idiom_name: three layers: asynchronous event demultiplexer, bounded queue, synchronous worker pool
implementation_notes: Language-neutral form: run one thread or event loop that does nothing but demultiplex external events and never blocks, push each unit of work into a bounded queue, and let a fixed pool of threads that own run-time stacks pull work from that queue and execute it with ordinary blocking calls. Keep the two layers' synchronisation policies separate - the demultiplexer uses non-blocking readiness or completion notification, the workers may block - and make the queueing layer the only place where buffering, notification and flow control happen. Every hand-off should carry an owned or immutable payload so no mutable state is shared across the boundary. Layer-to-layer flow control: synchronous tasks can block when the queue is full (they sleep), but the asynchronous layer cannot block, so it must discard or shed when the queue overflows.
code_sketch:
loop:                                   # asynchronous layer
    events = demultiplex(timeout=-1)    # epoll/kqueue/IOCP/select, never blocks on I/O
    for e in events: queue.push(decode(e))

workers:                                # synchronous layer
    payload = queue.pop()               # blocks when the queue is empty
    handle(payload)                     # may block on I/O, locks, databases
pitfalls: Forgetting that the demultiplexer must never block: a single blocking call in the asynchronous layer serialises every event source.
Leaving the queue unbounded, so overload becomes memory growth and latency instead of back-pressure.
Sharing mutable state across the boundary instead of passing messages through the queueing layer.
Blocking in the asynchronous layer — a blocking database or file call from the event loop — which stalls every event source and removes the pattern's QoS benefit.
Not implementing layer-to-layer flow control: synchronous tasks must block when the queue is full; the async layer must discard when it produces faster than the sync layer can drain.
Payload aliasing: passing a mutable pointer into the queue and then continuing to use it in the async layer before the worker has consumed it, causing data races on the buffer.
Excessive data copying at the user/kernel boundary: use shared memory regions between layers where possible to reduce bus and memory load.

Long-lived blocking tasks in the synchronous worker pool: pools sized for short hand-offs (Tokio's blocking pool, libuv's 4-thread default) starve when a task never finishes; run persistent blocking work on dedicated threads, not the shared queue's pool.

Marshalling every result back onto the single loop thread: if completion callbacks become the funnel through which all output flows, the asynchronous layer turns into the serialisation point the design was meant to remove.
sources: Schmidt, D. C. & Cranor, C. D., 'Half-Sync/Half-Async: An Architectural Pattern for Efficient and Well-structured Concurrent I/O,' PLoP 1995 / POSA 2, Addison-Wesley, 1996 — the definitive reference for the three-layer structure (async task layer, queueing layer, sync task layer) and the canonical BSD UNIX and CORBA ORB examples.

Lea, D., 'Scalable Synchronous Queues,' Communications of the ACM, Vol. 52, No. 5, May 2009 — background on wait-free and lock-free queue algorithms for the queueing layer, including the basis for java.util.concurrent SynchronousQueue.

Scherer, W. N. III, Lea, D. & Scott, M. L., 'Scalable Synchronous Queues,' ACM PODI/SPAA 2005 — the original lock-free queue paper underpinning many modern concurrent queue implementations used in HS-HA queueing layers.
